title: MENLO: From Preferences to Proficiency – Evaluating and Modeling Native-like Quality Across 47 Languages
claim: A multi-stage annotation pipeline turns human-written templates into localized prompts, rubrics, and rated response pairs across many languages.
layout: 4 stages, left-to-right, numbered captions below, thick arrows linking example boxes
description: A four-stage horizontal flow with a numbered caption under each stage. Stage 1 shows an English prompt template with highlighted placeholders [locale_nationality] and [locale_country]. A curved arrow leads to a diamond holding a document icon, labeled with the four dimensions: Localized Tone, Fluency, Tone and Localized Factuality. Stage 2 shows the Spanish translation of the prompt with the locale words highlighted. Below it are a speech bubble, a globe, stacked documents with German, French and Brazilian flags, and cultural icons such as a beer stein, the Eiffel Tower and a carnival dancer. Stage 3 shows a rubric table with 1–5 ratings from Major Failure to Excellent, and cascaded smaller rubric sheets with a pen icon. Stage 4 shows response pairs A and B with ratings of 4 and 5. LLM logos feed chat bubbles, and the stage ends with human annotation and check-mark or cross ratings. Blue text and flag colors give the accents.
caption: MENLO framework and annotation process. 1) Human-written prompt templates evoking local contexts are created in English for the four dimensions. 2) Prompt templates are translated and localized into 47 language varieties. 3) Annotation guidelines are created that break down each dimension into easy-to-follow rubrics. 4) LLMs are used to generate response pairs for each prompt, which are annotated with Likert-scale ratings and preferences.
abstract: Ensuring native-like quality of large language model (LLM) responses across many languages is challenging. To address this, we introduce MENLO, a framework that operationalizes the evaluation of native-like response quality based on audience design-inspired mechanisms. Using MENLO, we create a dataset of 6,423 human-annotated prompt-response preference pairs covering four quality dimensions with high inter-annotator agreement in 47 language varieties. Our evaluation reveals that zero-shot LLM judges benefit significantly from pairwise evaluation and our structured annotation rubrics, yet they still underperform human annotators on our dataset. We demonstrate substantial improvements through fine-tuning with reinforcement learning, reward shaping, and multi-task learning approaches. Additionally, we show that RL-trained judges can serve as generative reward models to enhance LLMs' multilingual proficiency, though discrepancies with human judgment remain. Our findings suggest promising directions for scalable multilingual evaluation and preference alignment. We release our dataset and evaluation framework to support further research in multilingual LLM evaluation (https://huggingface.co/datasets/facebook/menlo).
